Orchot Tzadikim 1:41: And he said further: it is no true worth of the soul for a king to be proud, how much more so for ordinary people, one toward another. And he told this: there was a king who sat upon his royal throne, and before him were thrones, one higher than the next. The king said to them: how have you seated yourselves, one above the other, without my permission? The uppermost one answered: the greatness of my family's lineage has seated me above my fellow. The second said: I have risen above the one below me because of my great wisdom. The third answered: the lowliness of my soul and the humility of my heart have seated me beneath them. And the king raised him up and made him great. And of this it is said (Proverbs 25:7), "for it is better that it be said to you, 'come up here,' than that you be put lower before a nobleman."
Orchot Tzadikim 1:42: At the time a person sees that the trait of pride is growing powerful over him, he must think thoughts that shake his heart: that he came from a putrid drop, and will return to dust and worms, and will have to give a reckoning before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He. And let him consider: how many proud men became proud and then passed from the world, forgotten, and became as though they had never existed at all — and what good did their pride do them?
Orchot Tzadikim 1:43: A fence for distancing oneself from pride and from other bad traits:
Orchot Tzadikim 1:44: One who wishes to uproot pride from his heart entirely cannot do this by thought alone; rather, he must first distance himself from haughtiness to the very furthest extreme. How so? A person who was accustomed to wearing important garments, made fancy like the garments of the coarse-spirited, and wishes to turn away from this — if he merely wears good garments and makes them moderate, he will not uproot pride from his heart by this. Or if it was his custom to seek honor and to strive for it in his words or in his other deeds, there is no remedy for this until he accustoms himself to great disgrace, sitting lower than everyone, and wearing tattered rags that shame their wearers, and the like of these things, until he uproots the haughtiness of heart from within him.
Orchot Tzadikim 1:45: And likewise one who is very quick to wrath and anger: at first he should accustom himself so that if he is struck or cursed, he will feel nothing at all, and he should walk this path for a long time, until he uproots the root of pride from himself; and then he should return and follow the middle path, and walk in it all his days. And in this way he should do with all bad traits: at first distance himself from the trait to the point where he can distance himself no further, and follow this practice for a long time, and then return and take hold of the middle path. And this matter is a complete remedy for all bad traits. And whoever's mind is drawn to serve the Blessed Creator in every single portion, in the choicest portion of it, should set this path before himself and before his fellow. And of this it is said (Psalms 50:23), "and to him that orders his way aright I will show the salvation of God."
Orchot Tzadikim 2:2: Humility is a good trait, and it is the opposite of pride. And whoever has this trait has already saved his soul from several kinds of evil. And whoever has attained this honored level performs a commandment and receives reward in proportion to the greatness of his humility, for humility is the root of divine service, and a small deed of the humble man is accepted before the Blessed Lord a thousand times more than a great deed of the proud man. And so our Sages said (Menachot 110a): whether one does much or little, so long as he directs his heart to Heaven. But a deed done out of pride is not accepted before the Blessed Lord, for it is an abomination of his soul, as it is said (Proverbs 16:5), "An abomination to the Lord is every haughty heart." And because of this, he cries out and is not answered, as it is said (Isaiah 1:15), "Even though you multiply prayer, I will not hear"; and they perform commandments, and they are flung back in their faces, as it is said (ibid. 1:12), "Who has required this of your hand, to trample My courts," and it is said (Jeremiah 7:21), "Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat flesh."
Orchot Tzadikim 2:3: But through the trait of humility and lowliness one attains all good, for "He gives grace to the humble" (Proverbs 3:34). And since he has found favor in the eyes of the Holy One, blessed be He, he cries out and is answered at once, as it is said (Isaiah 65:24), "Before they call, I will answer." And he performs commandments, and they are received with pleasure and joy, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 9:7), "for God has already accepted your works"; and not only that, but He desires them, as it is said (Malachi 3:4), "and the offering of Judah and Jerusalem shall be pleasant to the Lord."
Orchot Tzadikim 2:4: And what is humility? It is the submission and lowliness of the soul, regarding oneself as nothing. And a person is obligated in this at every time and every hour, to be lowly in his own eyes, of humble spirit, of tender heart, and of broken spirit. The root of humility is this: that even while he is at ease and secure, healthy and wealthy, and the Blessed Creator has done good to him, he should think that he is not deserving of it. And he should consider the greatness of God and the loftiness of His glory, and think: what am I? Am I not a very lowly creature, and am I not in a lowly and perishing world? And he should think: all the good deeds I am able to do are but a drop from the sea compared to what I am obligated to do. And he should do all his deeds for the honor of Heaven, and not to flatter any person, nor for any benefit, but should do everything for His great Name — this is the root of humility.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:5: But one who submits before the Blessed Creator only when his body or one of his limbs falls ill, or at the time his children and loved ones die, or at the time of his descent from his wealth and greatness, or when he grows old — truly, this humility and lowliness is always accepted before the Blessed Lord, but he has not thereby attained the essence of humility.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:6: And one is obligated to conduct himself with humility in business dealings with people in matters of money, going beyond the strict letter of the law with every person. And all his conduct with the world should be entirely with lowliness and gentleness. And the essence of humility is this: that he submit to those beneath him, such as his servants and the members of his household, and to those poor people who are sustained and benefit from him, whom he does not need and does not fear.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:7: One who submits to widows and converts and bears their burden and their trouble, and who hears his own disgrace and does not answer, out of the greatness of his humility — this is very true and upright humility.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:8: There is also another very good humility, such as one who submits before his teacher and before the wise and before the righteous who walk in upright ways, thinking to himself: these are the servants of the Blessed Lord, His attendants and those who love Him — and because of this he lowers himself before them and honors them. This too is good humility: to think, I will submit before the wise so that they will draw me near, teach me, and rebuke me, and lead me in the ways of the Blessed Lord. And there is another very good humility: that one submit before his own students and explain to them everything obscure, to the greater according to his greatness and to the lesser according to his smallness; and he should explain, and explain again, with a pleasant countenance, until they understand, and not say, "how can I keep answering him until he understands — is his heart not hard as stone?" Rather, he should go over the matter patiently, several times. And you already know the reward of Rabbi Preida, who repeated a lesson to one student four hundred times (Eruvin 54b).
Orchot Tzadikim 2:9: And there is yet another great humility: to learn from the young, and to seek from them what is hidden from him, and not to say, "how can I teach in front of this one, and how can I seek from him — is he not lesser than I?" And of this it is said, "from all my teachers I have gained understanding" (Psalms 119:99). And our Sages further said: be exceedingly, exceedingly humble in spirit before every person (Avot 4:4) — one must be humble in spirit not only before the great, but even before the small.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:10: And whoever walks in this path brings merit to the many, for he finds favor in the eyes of all who see him, and all his deeds and the manner of his conduct are accepted by them, and they constantly praise him, and through this they desire to do as he does, and every person will bless his son that he become like so-and-so — and by this he sanctifies the Blessed Name. But the proud man desecrates the Blessed Name and causes the many to sin, and he is like a carcass thrown in the marketplace, past which every passerby holds his hand over his nose until he has passed; so the proud man disgraces the Torah and those who study it, and drives people away from the Torah, for they say: what benefit is there in the Torah, seeing that those who study it are wicked? — and through this they separate themselves from the Torah.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:11: Humility is recognized in a person by six things:
Orchot Tzadikim 2:12: The first: by the intensity of a person's anger. For instance, if someone has greatly disgraced him in words or in deed, and he has cause to take revenge upon him, yet he rules over his own spirit and forgives him for the sake of the Blessed Creator — this is a sign of humility. But sometimes it is forbidden to forgive, such as when a Torah scholar has been disgraced in public, until the offender appeases him.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:13: The second: when great loss comes upon him, or his children and relatives die, and he justifies the judgment of the Blessed Creator upon him and accepts it out of love, as it is said (Leviticus 10:3), "and Aaron was silent" — this too demonstrates humility greatly.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:14: The third: if he hears that people praise him for his wisdom and his good deeds, he should not rejoice in his heart over this, but should think that his good deeds are few compared to what he is obligated to do, and are but a drop from the sea.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:15: And how much more so if they credit him with good deeds he did not do — he should not rejoice, but should be pained in his heart that a reputation has come to him for something he does not possess. And if someone relates bad things about him: if the matter is true, he should not seek to distort the truth in order to clear himself, as Judah said, "she is more righteous than I" (Genesis 38:26); and he should not endeavor to discredit the man who related it about him, nor hate him for having revealed the matter, but should submit to the Blessed Creator, who revealed a little out of much in order to chasten and rebuke him, so that he return to Him.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:16: And if what was related about him is false, he should not shame the one who related it, nor be angry with him. For there was once one of the sages about whom bad things were related, and when the matter became known to a certain pious man, he sent a gift to the one who had related it, and wrote to him: you have sent me a gift from your merits, and I have repaid you with this gift I have sent you. For on the Day of Judgment, commandments are shown to many people who did not perform those commandments, and they will say: did we not fail to do this?! And it will be answered them: those who related evil about you — they performed these commandments, and they are being taken from them and given to you.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:17: And likewise the wicked are shown transgressions they did not commit, and when they say, "did we not fail to do this?!" it will be answered them: those transgressions were committed by those about whom you spoke slander, and they have been taken from them and added to your account. And this is what is said (Psalms 79:12), "and render to our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom their reproach with which they have reproached You, O Lord" — for whoever reproaches the righteous is as though he reproaches the Blessed Lord Himself, for the enemies of Israel are called "enemies of the Lord" in several places. And of this we were warned in the Torah (Deuteronomy 24:9), "Remember what the Lord your God did to Miriam."
Orchot Tzadikim 2:18: Therefore whoever bears his own disgrace and remains silent is recognized as humble. And so we find with Hillel the Nasi (Shabbat 88b), regarding one who disgraced him, saying to him, "may there not be many like you in Israel!" — yet he took no offense (Shabbat 31a). And it is found in the Midrash: none is humble except one who hears his own disgrace and does not answer, as it is written (Numbers 12:1), "and Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses," and it is written (ibid. 12:3), "and the man Moses was very humble."
Orchot Tzadikim 2:19: And of them it is said (Judges 5:31), "and they who love Him shall be as the sun going forth in its might."
Orchot Tzadikim 2:20: The fourth: if the Blessed Creator does him good with wealth and children, and grants him extra wisdom, understanding, and honor, he should add still more humility and lowliness before the Blessed Creator, and should honor people and do good to them even more than before — as with Abraham, at the time the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, "Shall I hide from Abraham..." (Genesis 18:17), he said, "and I am dust and ashes" (ibid. 18:27).
Orchot Tzadikim 2:21: Great wisdom and great doubled wealth in this world come about because of one of three things:
Orchot Tzadikim 2:22: The first, for good, from the Holy One, blessed be He; the second, for a test; and the third, for retribution.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:23: The sign of it being for good: if this rich man does no harm to any person with his money, or the wise man does not use his wisdom cleverly to harm any person, but rather this one through his wisdom and that one through his wealth increase their service of the Holy One, blessed be He, each according to his own matter — then truly the wisdom or the wealth is for good, from the Holy One, blessed be He.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:24: And the sign of it being for a test is this: that the man of wealth is preoccupied with guarding his wealth, and fears lest he lose it, and does not enjoy his wealth by making use of it and eating from it, and also does not harm anyone with his wealth, and also does not become proud, but constantly toils to gather riches and worries over guarding them, and also does not give charity and has no compassion for the poor, neither feeding nor clothing them. And likewise the wise man: if he devotes most of his wisdom to this world, to arrange his own affairs, and does not use his cleverness either for evil or for good — these are certainly for a test.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:25: And the sign of it being for retribution: that the man of wealth harms others with his money, and becomes proud through it, and does no charity with it, and is preoccupied with it in order to indulge himself, as the verse says (Isaiah 22:13), "joy and gladness, slaying oxen and killing sheep"; and it says (ibid. 5:12), "and the harp and the lute, the tambourine and the flute and wine are at their feasts"; and he does not pay from it the due of the Holy One, blessed be He — of this it is said (Ecclesiastes 5:12), "riches kept by their owner to his hurt." And likewise if the wise man uses his cunning to do evil and does not do good, as it is said (Jeremiah 4:22), "they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge" — then his wisdom becomes a stumbling-block to him.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:26: Therefore, let the intelligent man do good with his wealth and his wisdom in proportion to the abundance of his wealth and wisdom. And let him add submission and lowliness, and not let his heart grow haughty; and let him always worry lest this wealth be his [full] reward, and that he be among those of whom it is said (Deuteronomy 7:10), "and repays those who hate Him to their face, to destroy them." And let the wise man too worry lest he be among those of whom it is said (Jeremiah 4:22), "they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge." And every person is obligated to use wisdom and to reflect, so that through his wisdom he attains good deeds, to the utmost limit of what his wisdom is capable of achieving.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:27: The fifth: when he reproaches himself for having done evil to a person, in deed or in word, and he no longer needs anything at all from that person and does not hope to receive any benefit from him; and he goes of his own accord, without others urging him, and asks his forgiveness, and humbles himself before him, and repairs what he has done wrong, and speaks words of supplication to him — this too is a sign of humility.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:28: The sixth: that he conduct himself with humility in gentle words, as it is said (Proverbs 15:1), "a soft answer turns away wrath"; and in a low voice, for this is the speech of lowliness, as it is said (Isaiah 29:4), "and you shall be brought down and speak out of the ground, and your speech shall be low out of the dust"; and he should not occupy himself with the beauty of garments and ornaments, as it is said (Job 22:29), "and He shall save the one of downcast eyes"; and he should not occupy himself with pleasures, as the matter is said (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul." All these are signs of humility.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:29: Humility is a ladder for climbing to the ways of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said (Psalms 25:9), "He guides the humble in justice, and teaches the humble His way." And from it one attains fear of the Blessed Lord, as it is said (Proverbs 22:4), "the reward of humility is the fear of the Lord." The Divine Presence rests upon the humble, as it is said (Isaiah 57:15), "I dwell with the crushed and the humble of spirit." The Holy One, blessed be He, inclined His Presence upon Mount Sinai and descended below, passing over all the high mountains. And it is written (ibid. 26:19), "Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust, for your dew is a dew of lights" — whoever becomes a neighbor of the dust in his lifetime in this world will live in the World to Come.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:30: And it is written (Psalms 138:6), "For though the Lord is high, yet He regards the lowly."
Orchot Tzadikim 2:31: And whoever regards his own heart as [mere] flesh — his prayer is heard (Sotah 5a), as it is written (Isaiah 66:23), "all flesh shall come to bow down before Me, says the Lord"; and it is written (Psalms 65:3), "O You who hears prayer, to You all flesh shall come."
Orchot Tzadikim 2:32: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: how great are the humble in spirit before the Holy One, blessed be He! For when the Temple stood, a person would offer a burnt-offering and receive the reward of a burnt-offering, or a meal-offering and receive the reward of a meal-offering; but whoever is of humble mind — the verse accounts it to him as though he had offered all the offerings, as it is said (Psalms 51:19), "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit." And not only that, but his prayer is never rejected, as it is said (ibid.), "a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise" (Sotah 5b).
Orchot Tzadikim 2:33: Many good branches grow from the root of humility: the humble man is patient, and from patience peace will come; and through humility he quiets the anger of one who is angry at him, as it is said (Proverbs 15:1), "a soft answer turns away wrath." And peace is a very good trait.
Orchot Tzadikim 2:34: The humble man has grace, as it is said (Proverbs 3:34), "and to the humble He gives grace." The humble man's prayer is accepted before the Holy One, blessed be He, for he overlooks the wrongs done to him. And because of this the prayer of Rabbi Akiva was accepted when he said, "Our Father, our King" (Ta'anit 25b). The humble man merits to attain wisdom, for he submits before the wise and rolls in the dust of their feet, and it is said (Proverbs 13:20), "he who walks with the wise shall become wise." The humble man is shown mercy from Heaven, as it is said (ibid. 28:13), "but he who confesses and forsakes [his sins] shall find mercy."
Orchot Tzadikim 2:35: The humble man flees from greatness and from honor, and on this depends modesty, as it is said (Micah 6:8), "and to walk humbly with your God."
